background.definition: Chancroid is a sexually transmitted disease characterized by painful genital ulceration and inflammatory inguinal lymphadenopathy resulting from infection with Haemophilus ducreyi.

list.listitem: Uncommon in the United States, with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reporting only 33 cases nationwide in 2006.
Eight states reported at least one case.
Four states (New York, North Carolina, South Carolina, and Texas) reported more than one case.
H. ducreyi, a small, fastidious, Gram-negative rod.
H. ducreyi is sexually transmitted by direct contact. Incubation period is 1 day to 2 weeks.
Cytocidal toxins are released by bacterium, producing ulcerations.
The disease generally begins as a small papule that progresses to a deep painful ulcer within days. Painful inguinal adenopathy ensues and, if left untreated, may form suppurative buboes.
Condom use is thought to reduce the risk of chancroid. B
There is conflicting evidence on whether circumcision is associated with a lower risk of chancroid. B
Chancroid is characterized by painful genital ulceration (1-2 cm with an erythematous base) and inflammatory inguinal lymphadenopathy. C
Obtain culture or PCR for herpes simplex virus and serology for syphilis on all patients with genital ulcers. C
Culture is insensitive, and PCR, though very sensitive for H. ducreyi, is usually not performed on site, causing significant delays in receiving results. B

Differential.Differential_Features: Painful, deep, purulent ulcer; tender inguinal adenopathy
Painful, shallow ulcerations; begin vesicular; recurrent
Ulcers healing spontaneously in 2-3 days, followed by painful inguinal adenopathy

list.listitem: Patients with chancroid generally present with a history of a small erythematous papule that rapidly evolves into a pustule that then ulcerates.

Ulcers are generally 1-2 cm, painful, and with an erythematous base. Borders are well demarcated and sometimes undermined. Ulcers are typically covered in a gray to yellow exudate and usually bleed when scraped.
The classic clinical picture of a deep, undermined, painful, purulent ulcer is only 34% sensitive but 94% specific.
Infected persons commonly develop more than 1 ulcer.
Infection is generally confined to the genitals and the draining lymph nodes.
Inguinal lymphadenitis is present in approximately 50% of men, but is less common in women.
H. ducreyi is difficult to isolate from culture.
PCR is much more sensitive than culture and is the preferred test if available.
Suspect chancroid in patients with ulcerating genital papules. Culture of H. ducreyi is not necessary for diagnosis of chancroid.
All patients with genital ulcers should have serology for syphilis as well as a diagnostic evaluation for herpes, in addition to testing for other potential STDs.

Because of difficulty in diagnosing chancroid, the CDC developed two diagnostic criteria: “Definite chancroid” is positive culture of H. ducreyi from the lesion, whereas “probable chancroid” is clinical symptoms consistent with chancroid plus negative serologic testing for syphilis and negative culture for herpes.
Single-dose oral therapies recommended by CDC include azithromycin 1 gm orally and ceftriaxone 250 mg IM. AB
Other treatment options include IM ciprofloxacin 500 mg orally twice daily for 3 days or erythromycin 500 mg orally 3 times daily for 7 days. B
Single-dose oral therapies recommended by CDC include azithromycin 1 gm orally (91% cure rate) and ceftriaxone 250 mg IM.
Other treatment options recommended by CDC include ciprofloxacin 500 mg orally twice daily for 3 days or erythromycin 500 mg orally 3 times daily for 7 days.

A single dose of ciprofloxacin 500 mg (92%) was found to be as effective as erythromycin in a study in Kenya in 1999, but this is not endorsed by CDC. Resistance has to ciprofloxacin and erythromycin has been reported.
Re-examine patients 3 to 7 days after therapy. If treatment is successful, ulcers generally improve by 3 days symptomatically and objectively in a week.
A Cochrane review found weak evidence suggesting that single dose azithromycin is the preferred therapy.
Other regimens include ceftriaxone 250 mg injected IM (88%) and ciprofloxacin 500 mg orally twice per day for 3 days (100%).
Patients coinfected with HIV are less likely to respond to therapy.
Ulcers symptomatically improve within 3 days and objectively improve within 7 days of treatment. B
Consider coinfection with other sexually transmitted infections or drug resistance in patients not improving. C
Healing is slower for uncircumcised men with ulcers under the foreskin. C
Resolution of adenopathy is slower than that for ulcers and may require incision and drainage. C
Ciprofloxacin is contraindicated in pregnancy.
Both azithromycin and ceftriaxone are pregnancy category B.
